speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I would like to make an announcement about the government's program for assisting NATO countries to set up strategic stockpiles of wheat flour.
Hon. members will recall that on June 1 of last year the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) informed the house, as reported at page 4189 of Hansard, of the government's intention to ask parliament for $10 million for that purpose. He recalled how he had brought forward at the meeting of heads of governments of NATO countries at Paris in December, 1957 a proposal for the establishment of a food bank among the NATO countries for use in the event of an outbreak of hostilities. He expressed at that time the willingness of the Canadian government to play its part in the establishment of such food reserves. The house was made aware of the facts of the matter on July 19, 1958 during the debate on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Later, in October of that year, 1958, the terms of the Canadian offer were made known in detail to our NATO allies. During the course of last year, as the Prime Minister reported, discussions were carried on with interested countries, but these took longer than we had expected and no agreements were reached in time to enable us to make use of the $10 million voted for the last fiscal year. However, I am now able to announce, and I do so with pleasure, that an agreement was concluded yesterday with Norway under which Canada will provide
20,000	tons of wheat flour later this year for wartime emergency stockpiling purposes in Norway. In due course, when the supplementary estimates of my department for this year

External Affairs
come before the house, an item will be included to cover the expenditures that will be involved in this agreement.
The agreement with Norway took the form of an exchange of notes between myself and the Norwegian ambassador. These set out the terms and conditions under which the wheat flour will be provided by Canada and stored by Norway. With your leave I wish to table copies of the notes.
Briefly, the agreement provides that 20,000 tons of flour suitably packaged for long storage will be delivered to Canadian seaports to be specified by the government, and that Norway will inspect and assume title to the flour at those ports with all expenses thereafter being borne by the Norwegian government. They will transport the flour to Norway where they will store it for emergency wartime use. When it is no longer fit for human consumption it will be replaced by Norway either by wheat or wheat flour so as to maintain the original level of the stockpile at 20,000 tons.
I may perhaps add that the ambassador of Norway expressed to me his government's appreciation for Canada's contribution to their food stockpile within the framework of our common NATO defence objectives.
Mr. Speaker, I would now ask leave to table copies of these notes.

number of hon. members have recently expressed interest in the meetings which have been held lately by the unemployment insurance advisory committee dealing with regulations 172 and 173. I have also received a number of submissions in connection with this matter, and inquiries as to the effect of these regulations. In view of the interest thus shown I would seek the indulgence of the house at this time to make a brief statement.
As the house knows, the regulations were recently considered by the advisory committee, which then reported to the unemployment insurance commission. Holiday pay will continue to be regarded as earnings in the case of a general plant shutdown for holidays occurring within six weeks of a claimant's separation from employment. speechtext: I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he would care to comment on the situation which has arisen at the conference on the law of the sea at Geneva, where the Canadian proposal was defeated yesterday so narrowly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subtopic: CONFERENCE ON LAW OF THE SEA-DEFEAT OF CANADIAN PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will have seen the press reports concerning today's vote at the law of the sea conference, at which by the narrow margin of one vote-in fact I think it was
Inquiries of the Ministry a percentage of a vote-the joint Canada-United States proposal failed to gain the necessary two thirds majority. The vote was 54 in favour and 28 against with 5 abstentions.
Efforts were made immediately after the vote to have the proposal reconsidered, but the motion for reconsideration was also defeated by a very narrow margin. As a result the conference has terminated without having arrived at a conclusion of any kind, and the international community is now left without agreement on a rule of law on the territorial sea and Ashing limits. Naturally the government will now have to consider what action might have to be taken in the light of this failure.
I should like to pay tribute to Hon. George Drew, who led the Canadian delegation, and all his colleagues for the vigorous way in which they have dedicated themselves during the weeks of the conference and indeed for many months before in working for a formula which would provide for the orderly development of international law in this important held.
During the conference, as hon. members know, we reached a compromise with the United States and together with that country Canada has carried out one of the most extensive diplomatic campaigns we have ever undertaken in an effort to line up the necessary support. We have done everything possible to achieve a positive result. Both those in Geneva and in our missions abroad who worked toward this end deserve the highest commendation.
There has been one feature with regard to the Canada-United States compromise plan which I think has been misunderstood across the country. In the original Canadian plan we advocated a six-mile territorial limit and then a six-mile excluded Ashing zone. The United States brought forward the same proposal with the proviso that in the outer six miles the so-called historic rights would continue in perpetuity. Canada has been willing to negotiate bilaterally or on a multilateral basis with countries Ashing within twelve miles of our shores for a phasing-out period of these so-called historic rights. The compromise reached was that a ten-year period for phasing-out would be written into the convention.
The inference has been taken by some papers in Canada that we were willing to negotiate for a period beyond ten years; that is to say, perhaps for twenty years. But this was never the intention. We had been willing originally to negotiate for a period certainly not greater than ten years and preferably less; then when the compromise was reached

Inquiries of the Ministry the only change made was that that was to be written right into the convention rather than being negotiated. At no time was there any intention to have the so-called historic rights last for longer than ten years.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one conservationist to another I want to fire a double-barrelled question, purely for exploratory purposes, to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
My question is based on a report in this morning's Globe and Mail which indicates that a certain Mr. Elmhurst suggests that some of his hardwood timber has suffered considerable loss over the years from the depradations of great blue herons, which are migratory birds. He has been given a permit by someone authorizing him to shoot or otherwise destroy the birds. Since he is a good conservationist he refuses to do this.
My questions are first, who has the authority to issue permits for the destruction of migratory birds? Second, will the minister have this case investigated to make certain of the continued protection of these great


blue herons, and also to see whether some arrangements can be made for compensation to this worthy conservationist?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS
subtopic: MIGRATORY BIRDS
speechtext:
I should like to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question.
Under the Migratory Birds Convention Act and regulations the chief game officer of a province or, in certain circumstances, game officers appointed under the provisions of the act may issue permits for the destruction of migratory birds that are causing or are likely to cause serious damage to crops or other interests.
With regard to the second part, there has been an exchange of correspondence between Ontario and the Canadian wildlife service on this matter. The service has recommended that, when the birds come in the spring, attempts to scare them should first be made. If this is unsuccessful and damage continues, some of the birds could be killed under permit in order to protect this man's property.
I assure the hon. member that we will look into this matter further to ensure the observance of the best interests of the conservation of migratory birds, having regard also for the protection of private property from damage.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-56, to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to repeat anything that was said at the resolution stage of this amendment. That resolution has already been the subject of a two-day debate, on March 18 and again on April 1. The resolution received the unanimous approval of the house. I thank the house for that approval and for the approving comments that were made in connection with the alternative basis proposed in relation to university grants. I hope the house will be able now to accord the same unanimous support to the bill.
Briefly, the bill has two features. The first concerns the increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax. That increase will, by the terms of this bill, become effective now until March 31, 1962.
The second feature of the bill concerns the alternative basis in relation to university grants. The statute as it is proposed to be amended will make provision for the payment of university grants equivalent to $1.50 per head of population in each province. If this bill is adopted, item 125 of the main estimates for the current fiscal year will be withdrawn. In the second place the provision becomes affective now on a statutory basis for two years. Hitherto it has been on an annual basis only, simply by reason of an item in the estimates.
The third comment concerns the alternative method that is now available to any province. The bill also makes provision for power to be given to revise any tax-sharing agreement which any province has entered into in the event that it now desires to resume the collection of the corporation tax for one or both of the two remaining years of the current five-year period under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act.
I comment on only one matter that was raised in debate at the resolution stage. Attention was drawn to the fact that those who

now constitute the government and its supporters in the house did not support this measure when it was introduced by the former administration in 1956; and yet, having come into office, the agreements that were entered into in pursuance of that statute have been continued in force and have been fully recognized by the government.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we did not support this measure when it was introduced in the house in 1956. Indeed, we voted against it, and we divided the house on the bill. But I would point out, as I have had occasion to do in former debates, that in pursuance of the terms of this enactment, agreements were entered into by the former federal government with nine of the provincial governments. When we came into office and since then we have fully honoured and carried out the terms of those agreements and will, of course, continue to do so during the full period they are in force up to March 31, 1962. We are not the kind of people who repudiate agreements that have been entered into in pursuance of legislation passed by the parliament of Canada. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we have greatly improved, for the benefit of the provinces, the terms upon which nine provinces entered into these agreements, and we have made those improvements for the benefit of the ten provinces both with respect to the tax rental features of the agreements and the principle of equalization which was written into the bill in order to aid the fiscally weaker provinces.
We made those improvements at the expense of our own federal fiscal position at a time when we were incurring deficits. I point out that this bill, if now adopted, will assure to the provinces for the balance of the present quinquennial period to March 31, 1962, the benefit of the increased federal payments.
Finally, the house is aware that the Prime Minister has invited the premiers of all of the provinces to meet in a plenary dominion-provincial conference to be held in Ottawa on July 25, 26 and 27 next. The continuing committee of officials drawn from both federal and provincial governments, which has done such useful work from which the ministers of finance and provincial treasurers at their meetings held in July and October of 1957 derived much benefit, will be invited to meet in advance of the plenary conference.
The matters to be submitted to the conference will concern financial relations between the dominion and the provinces in the period following March 31, 1962. It is therefore not anticipated that, if the house sees

fit to adopt the present bill, further amendments to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act will be required during the balance of the present period to March 31, 1962.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance stated that there was not much that he intended to add to what had already been said on the resolution. However, he reiterated some of the statements he made on that occasion and added one or two additional remarks which I do not believe change the substance of what he said during the course of the debate on the resolution. So this leaves the position, in so far the as the principle of this bill is concerned, exactly where it was when the discussion on the resolution terminated.
I would like to deal with this bill in several of its aspects, but before doing so I would like to say something with reference to the historical and constitutional aspects of the situation. In 1950 all Canadian universities requested from the federal government financial assistance with respect to their position as it was then found, and these representations were made to the Massey commission. The Massey commission was impressed by the representations which were made to it. It was impressed not only because of the need of the universities at the time and because of the fact that the representations pointed to the responsibility of the federal government in this sphere, but because there is no doubt that without any exception all Canadian universities at the time felt that assistance should be forthcoming.
So in 1951 the Massey commission made representations to this effect to the then government, and the government of Mr. St. Laurent accepted those recommendations and a special item providing for direct federal grants to universities was included in the 1951-52 estimates. All present Conservative members who were sitting on this side of the house at that time supported the measure.
Thereafter consultations were held with the provinces, and as a result of these consultations all provincial governments accepted the idea of direct federal grants to universities for the year 1951-52. So that what appears today to the Quebec Conservatives as a crime committed by the St. Laurent government was approved in the fiscal year 1951-52 first by all Canadian universities, next by all provincial governments, and also by all political parties in this house including the Conservative party. Therefore when the Quebec members accuse the St. Laurent government, they must not forget for one moment 79951-0-207J
26, 1960	3279
Dominion-Provincial Relations that they are also blaming their own party, including, of course, the present Prime * Minister and the Minister of Finance, who were enthusiastic accessories to the so-called crime of constitutional infringement.
Now I come quickly to 1956. It became evident to the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, in that year that the amount which had been put in the estimates in 1951-52 was not sufficient and that the universities would require greater assistance, including those in the province of Quebec. Mr. St. Laurent therefore proposed to double the grants, and he asked the national conference of Canadian universities to assume the responsibility for distributing the money to each university so as to make sure that any interference by the federal government with the freedom of individual universities would be absolutely impossible.
Again all Canadian universities accepted Mr. St. Laurent's proposal, but this time the Prime Minister added another feature by providing that the funds would accumulate if a university decided to refuse the grants temporarily, and as a result of that provision the sum of $25 million has been accumulated for Quebec universities since 1956. I am sure those universities are today very grateful to Mr. St. Laurent for making that provision, because otherwise it would not have been possible for them to recoup the millions of dollars which then would have been lost.
When the new proposal was introduced in the house by the former government early in 1957 it was again approved by all political parties, including the Conservative party. The Quebec Conservative members should not forget the attitude taken then by their own party. For the second time, in 1957 as in 1952, Quebec universities had to refuse the annual federal grants after having approved the formula. Again they feared retaliatory measures by the Quebec government. This becomes quite evident when we realize that all universities outside Quebec, including French speaking and Catholic institutions, accepted federal assistance. That I think is a point which hon. members on the other side of the house, particularly from the province of Quebec, seem to forget.
This deadlock was also recognized by the present government, which during more than two years in office did absolutely nothing to solve the problem. Last October hon. Mr. Sauve took the initiative and started negotiations with the federal government. Because of his action a solution became possible, and the Minister of Finance acknowledged his contribution when he paid tribute to him in his speech in this house at the resolution stage.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
So much lor the historical aspect of the situation. I now turn my remarks to the constitutional aspect. Here I state, sir, without any equivocation that there is a clear and profound division of opinion on this question within the ranks of the Conservative party. There is a division of opinion on the one hand in so far as the older members of the Conservative party are concerned and, on the other hand, in so far as the newly elected members from the province of Quebec are concerned. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the older Conservatives maintain that federal grants to universities are perfectly constitutional and that they should continue to be provided. On the contrary the newly elected Conservatives from Quebec argue that such grants are unconstitutional and that they are a clear violation of the constitution.
There is only one group which thus far has remained silent in the house on the issue, and that is the Quebec ministers in the government. Not one of them during the course of these debates which have come up in the house from time to time has had a word to say on this very important subject. The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) have never uttered a word on this important matter in the house. As representatives of the province of Quebec in the cabinet they have a clear obligation to participate in this debate, and they must now define their attitude in this respect.
The Quebec ministers cannot avoid the issue. This bill provides for federal grants to universities, and they will have to take a definite stand when they vote on it. The only honourable course for them to follow under such conditions, it seems to me-and I say this with all deference-is to define and justify their attitude before they express it by their vote. Therefore we shall anticipate' their participation in this debate with great interest.
I said a moment ago that the views of the older Conservatives were that federal grants to universities were perfectly constitutional. This cannot be disputed in any way whatsoever when one considers the attitude which was taken in 1951 and 1957 when those hon. members were in opposition; and since they have become members of the present government the introduction of this bill, for that matter, is another manifestation of those views which were clearly expressed by the
[Mr. Chevrier.)
Minister of Finance in this house on September 6, 1958 and again on March 18, 1960. The minister spoke in French when he said:
(Translation):
This government scrupulously respects the terms of the Canadian constitution and will always do. It is plainly recognized that education is a field of jurisdiction exclusively assigned to the provinces. The increased grants proposed by the government are merely a needed assistance to universities without any interference in any provincial field intended by the government.
(Text):
This can be found on page 2227 of Hansard. Such a statement could not be simpler or more clear, for the Minister of Finance, speaking twice on behalf of the present government, said that federal grants constitute a necessary assistance to universities and that the government does not thereby intervene in any provincial field. The Liberal party has expressed exactly similar views since 1951. The difference between ourselves and the Conservative party is that we have had the honesty and courage to make this statement from one end of the country to the other, including the province of Quebec. This is exactly what I said when I spoke in the house on July 18, 1959, as will be found on page 6678 of Hansard, and I quote:
(Translation):
Since they were established in 1951 we have always said that such grants were constitutional.
(Text):
For having said exactly what the Minister of Finance stated on September 6, 1958 and repeated on March 18, 1960, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) chose to attack me as appears at page 2809 of Hansard, when he spoke on the resolution preceding this bill on April 1, 1960. I have only one question to ask the hon. member for Bellechasse, and it is this. Why did he not have the courage to attack the Minister of Finance and his own party when he spoke in the house on April 1, instead of attempting to convince the house that he was opposed only to the point of view adopted by the Liberals?
The Minister of Finance made a very important statement twice in this house; that the federal government is not intervening in a provincial field when it makes university grants. I hope that in the course of this debate the Quebec Conservative members will address their constitutional objections to him, and ask the Minister of Finance to justify the position he holds in this respect. Even the hon. member for Bellechasse was at pains, and in an embarrassing position,

the other day when asked to reply to a question by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), when he stated that the Quebec government had the constitutional right to give financial assistance to universities outside Quebec. I am in agreement with the hon. member on this; but if the Quebec government can vote -and I quote his words-grants to universities outside Quebec at the request of those universities and with the consent of the governments of those provinces-and this quotation may be found on page 2813 of Hansard -although it has no jurisdiction whatsoever over education outside Quebec, then surely the federal parliament has the prerogative of voting similar grants to universities in any province without interfering in any way with the exclusive right of the provincial legislatures over education. The only constitutional limitations on such federal grants are that the federal government cannot finance them through a specific direct tax, and that it cannot use such assistance to impose compulsory regulations in educational matters or to encroach on the exclusive provincial jurisdiction in that field.
This was the position adopted by Mr. St. Laurent, and it is the position we are taking today. So far as the Liberal party is concerned we shall never tolerate any encroachment into this exclusive provincial field. The newly elected members from the province of Quebec still claim, however, that federal grants to universities are clearly a violation of the constitution.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
This provides for federal grants to universities according to the St. Laurent formula, which the hon. member and his friends so violently opposed during the last electoral campaigns in Quebec. The only difference is that this grant, instead of being provided for by a vote in the estimates, will from now on be paid as a statutory item. This change, however, establishes these grants on a much more permanent basis than before. The government has stated its intention, and in fact this intention has been confirmed by the statement the minister made a few
26. 1960	3281
Dominion-Provincial Relations moments ago, that these grants will be carried on until March, 1962 notwithstanding the dominion-provincial conference to be held next July.
The fact that Quebec universities will not receive the grants on the basis of the earlier formula does not change the constitutional position in any way. In other words, if a formula is a clear violation of the constitution, the fact that it will not apply in one province does not make it constitutional, and all hon. members of this house have the obligation of preserving the constitution not only in their respective provinces but in the whole of Canada. The Quebec Conservative members, no matter how hard they try, cannot escape this responsibility.
Now I should like to come to the formula which is to be found in the bill, and to discuss it in a general way. I claim that the formula as found in the bill does not solve the constitutional issue which exists at present according to the Quebec Conservative members. On the contrary, as I will show later, it raises new and much more serious constitutional difficulties of its own.
At this stage, however, I should like to show that the new formula, like the present one, provides for federal grants for the purpose of education. The essential difference between the two formulae resides in the fact that they follow two different methods of distribution of the same federal grants.
Indeed, the Minister of Finance has always been consistent and frank in this matter. He believes that federal grants are constitutional. He never intended to abolish them, though he was prepared to change the method of distribution. That is what he said on September 6, 1958, and what he repeated on the resolution preceding this bill:
I emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that in reference to this subject of the basis of distribution this present government makes no rigid approach. We adopt no take it or leave it attitude in regard to this basis of distribution.
Those words may be found at page 2227 of Hansard of March 18, 1960. In other words what the Minister of Finance said was this. We intend to continue to provide federal grants to help Canadian universities, but we are prepared to modify their method of distribution. That is exactly what the minister is doing in this bill. Here again he has been very clear and frank, when he said in introducing the resolution as reported at page 2225 of Hansard of March 18, 1960:
The amendment proposed will simply provide alternative arrangements so that grants now paid by the federal government to institutions of higher

Dominion-Provincial Relations learning under the authority of the annual Appropriation Act can be paid out of the federal treasury through the Canadian universities foundation under the authority of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act or, under certain circumstances, when a province so desires directly, by that province.
Therefore, according to the Minister of Finance himself, the bill provides for university grants paid out of the federal treasury. In the one case these federal grants will be paid through the Canadian universities foundation and in the other through the province. The fact that such federal grants will be made to universities through the Canadian universities foundation or through the province does not in any way modify the constitutional position in this respect. According to the new method embodied in this bill the university grants will be paid out of the federal treasury through a tax abatement not exceeding $1.50 per capita and, if necessary, through a straight conditional payment to the provincial government.
The constitutional position in so far as section 93 is concerned is not changed or altered in any way by this bill. If, as the Quebec Conservative members claim, the federal government does not have the power to provide grants to universities, then this bill is clearly unconstitutional and ultra vires. These Quebec Conservative members have no escape, therefore; because surely no pretext can be used to justify the violation of the constitution. However, as I said earlier, there is a new constitutional problem created by this bill.
While the new method of distribution does not remove in any way the constitutional issue raised by the Quebec Conservative members in regard to the present basis of distribution it does pose a new and, in my opinion, a genuine constitutional difficulty. This problem is related to section 92 of the constitution, which provides that-
-in each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to ... direct taxation within the province in order to the raising of a revenue for provincial purposes.
The press release issued by the Prime Minister on December 10, 1959 contains the following statement which has been embodied in this bill:
If the government of a province requests the change to be made in respect of that province, and undertakes to provide additional grants to the universities in that province on a scale equivalent to the present federal grants of $1.50 per capita, then parliament will be asked to authorize an increase of 1 per cent in the abatement made in the federal corporation tax in respect of that

province, from 9 per cent to 10 per cent. This increased allowance for a provincial corporation tax would be in lieu of federal grants for universities in that province. It would be necessary for the provincial legislature then to impose an additional corporation tax equivalent to the reduction in the federal tax and to authorize the payment of the additional grants to the universities.
In other words, the federal government in this bill is saying to a province "We will reduce our corporation income tax, which is a direct tax, by 1 per cent on the following conditions. The provincial government must levy a direct tax of at least 1 per cent on corporation income; the proceeds of that provincial tax must be distributed to the universities in the province, and the total grant must not be less than $1.50 per capita. If the proceeds of that tax exceed $1.50 per capita we, the federal government, will appropriate the surplus of those provincial revenues."
Under such conditions the federal government determines when a provincial tax will be levied, what will be its minimum rate, how it will be utilized for a provincial purpose, and what will be its maximum yield to the provincial treasury. For all practical purposes, therefore, as the Minister of Finance has said, university grants will be paid out of the federal treasury by the province.
But that is not the whole story. In addition, the arrangement to be made by the province with the universities will have to be in accordance with and subject to terms and conditions not inconsistent with those contained in any agreement entered into between the Minister of Finance and the Canadian universities foundation. Therefore the provincial government, in distributing its own money to universities within the province, will have to comply with conditions set out in an agreement to which it is not even a party and which will be determined, for all practical purposes, unilaterally by the Minister of Finance.
Finally, the Minister of Finance will be the only judge to determine whether the arrangements made by the provincial government with the universities within the province are satisfactory.
This is, to say the least, a fantastic piece of legislation. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that no other federal government or minister of finance since confederation has dared to intervene so emphatically, so evidently and so thoroughly in an exclusively provincial matter. The way a provincial government

deals with universities within the province is not in any way the concern of the federal government. Under the proposed arrangement, however, the provincial government is not even in the same position as the Canadian universities foundation, which will at least have the opportunity to discuss the terms of its agreement with the Minister of Finance. The province will become a mere fiscal agent of the federal authority with respect to a direct provincial tax raised for a provincial purpose.
This arrangement amounts to a delegation by the federal government of a provincial power to a provincial government. This is surely the height of arrogance, because our courts have decided that even the delegation of a federal power to a legislature or vice versa was unconstitutional.
In this connection I would like to quote from a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, the case of the attorney general of Nova Scotia et al v. the Attorney General of Canada et al, found at page 369 of Dominion Law Reports, volume 4, 1950. I should like to read just one sentence from the headnote and then a portion of the judgment of Mr. Justice Estey. The headnote of this case reads in part as follows:
Neither the parliament of Canada nor the legislature of any province can delegate one to the other (to be exercised by that other as a parliament or legislature, as the case may be) any of the legislative authority respectively conferred upon them by the British North America Act and especially by sections 91 and 92 thereof.
At page 391 Mr. Justice Estey, among other things, had this to say:
Moreover, the provisions of the British North America Act contemplate these legislative bodies will, at all times, in the exercise of their sovereign jurisdiction, act as principals. There is no express provision nor is there any under which it could be reasonably implied that these bodies were intended to act as agents one for the other.
It would appear that the position which I have been taking is confirmed by a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada.
According to the provisions of the present bill the provincial government will, for all practical purposes, act as agent for the federal government but in a provincial field. The new scheme, therefore, raises a very serious constitutional issue which is related to the exclusive right of the provinces to raise direct taxes for provincial purposes and to spend the proceeds as the legislature see fit. Our courts have already decided that the federal government and the provinces do not
26. 1960
Dominion-Provincial Relations have the right to surrender by mutual consent a prerogative or a responsibility assigned to them by the constitution. If a province cannot transfer its exclusive constitutional powers to the federal government, it cannot by implication accept any specific limitation on the exercise of those powers imposed by parliament as the condition of an arrangement, because such limitation would amount to the partial surrender of those powers to parliament.
I have grave doubts about the constitutionality of the new arrangement embodied in this bill. I am not, of course, competent enough in constitutional matters to be sure that this new scheme is, in fact, ultra vires in its entirety, but I am quite confident that it is at least incompatible with the spirit of our constitution.
Moreover, there is another feature in the arrangement contained in this bill which appears to be an encroachment on the exclusive taxation powers of provincial legislatures. This is the provision:
"There may be deducted from any payment to the province under this act or otherwise recovered as a debt due to Canada by the province, any amount by which one ninth of the standard corporation income tax as applied to the province for that fiscal year exceeds an amount calculated by multiplying the population of the province for the calendar year ending in that fiscal year by one dollar and fifty cents."
In other words, the federal government asserts under this provision that if the yield of the additional provincial tax of 1 per cent exceeds $1.50 per head, the excess of that provincial tax raised for a provincial purpose belongs to the federal government and will be recovered as a debt due to the federal treasury by the province. This, it seems to me, is a violation of section 92 of the constitution. Under our constitutional provisions the federal government does not have access to direct taxation raised for a provincial purpose. Such taxation raised for a provincial purpose belongs exclusively to the provinces. Moreover, revenues raised by a province under section 92 belong to the legislature of that province exclusively, and the federal government cannot claim any share of such revenues in the form of deductions or otherwise as if those were a debt due by the province to the federal treasury.
Here I should like to substantiate the opinion I express by a Supreme Court of Canada decision in 1930 in the reference "Troops in Cape Breton". The court, at page 562 of its 1930 reports, had this to say:
The Solicitor General in his very candid argument did not contend that the duty to pay these

Dominion-Provincial Relations expenses could be imposed by the dominion on the province in invitum and that, of course, would be a plain violation of the fundamental principle of the British North America Act. The revenues of the province are vested in His Majesty as the supreme head of the province, and the right of appropriation of all such revenues belongs to the legislature of the province exclusively.
The provision authorizing the deduction of moneys due by a province under these sections from the annual subsidy does not help the dominion. Obviously such a deduction could not constitutionally be made, unless the province was under an obligation to pay.
It is quite evident, therefore, that a share of provincial revenues produced by direct taxation, such as a corporation income tax, and raised for a provincial purpose, namely education, cannot be claimed as a debt due to the federal treasury by a province. Moreover, since there is no such debt, the province has no obligation to pay the amount claimed by the federal government. And since the province has no obligation to pay, the deduction that the federal government intends to make under the terms of this bill cannot constitutionally be made, as the Supreme Court of Canada has already pointed out in the decision of 1930.
It has been said that this bill is an improvement over the present situation, and that it is a step in the right direction. I certainly cannot agree with these views. On the contrary, I believe that several provisions of this bill constitute the worst intrusion ever attempted by a federal government in the affairs of a province. From that point of view I feel that it establishes a very bad precedent and that it is a step in the wrong direction.
In conclusion I should like to summarize the attitude of the official opposition toward the main parts of this bill. We support the increased payment to the provinces; that is, the extension of the rate of 13 per cent of the standard individual income tax for a further period of two years, although such an arrangement is not what the provinces were led to believe they would get from the present government before the last general election. Next, we are also in favour of the university grants paid out of the federal treasury, which were started by a Liberal government, and distributed through the Canadian universities foundation or, as I suggested last year, through a provincial universities foundation or council, because such grants are in the public interest; they are not financed by a specific direct tax, and they are not accompanied by any conditions affecting education.
So far as the constitutional basis of the proposed new arrangement for federal financial aid to universities through the provinces

is concerned, we believe this is an attempt to go beyond the jurisdiction of parliament. We do not feel that anyone in this house should be an accessory to what seems to us a violation of the constitution, even if such violation were to last for a period of only two years. Therefore we feel that the government should either satisfy the house that the bill is completely constitutional or give us an assurance that the necessary modifications will be made during the course of the discussion to bring the bill within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament.

Besides, why should we have entrusted to provincial governments the exclusive power of looking after education, if the educational system had been the same in all the provinces which were to become members of the confederation?
Nobody will dare deny that the British North America Act, pact or contract, is a modus vivendi between French-speaking Canadians and English-speaking Canadians.
One has only to read the text of the constitution to realize that the fathers of confederation wanted the province of Quebec to be different from the others, with, for instance, its fixed provincial constituencies where English-speaking voters were in the majority at the time.
In their formula, the Liberals had overlooked historical facts, so vivid in the province of Quebec, with the result that even if English-speaking provinces could obtain the millions collected by Ottawa to provide assistance to universities, the people of Quebec were being taxed like all the others while its universities were compelled to turn down the largesses of the federal government.
People outside the French province, wondered when they found that, year after year, Quebec leaders were turning down federal grants. Our opponents went so far as to describe that attitude as "segregationism" but it was the Liberals, with their anticonstitutional formula, who applied a policy of intellectual segregation with regard to Quebec.
I would even say that they are responsible for the little anti-Quebec outbreak of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who, after all, only repeated in 1960 what the Liberals, for the last four years of their regime, had been saying to anybody who

Dominion-Provincial Relations would listen. At the time when the university grants bill was introduced, the Liberals had come to believe that every evil which fell upon this country could only be blamed on the Quebec voters. At that time the Liberals did not dare to launch a straightforward attack against the hon. Mr. Duplessis and his autonomist policies. They relieved their feelings by attacking the province of Quebec of which Mr. Duplessis obviously had become the living symbol.
To stand well with the federal ministers from Quebec, it was necessary at the time to miss no opportunity to refer with pity or disdain to the backward French province which, it was claimed, was keeping to itself; where it was said people did not understand the general progress of Canada; where people allegedly refused to keep abreast of other Canadians. It was then that there was launched the famous formula from very high quarters and without the slightest provocation, after all the province of Quebec is a province like all the others.
Therefore, the hon. member for Port Arthur, who knows nothing about Quebec, only repeated in his own words, in 1960, what government members said in Ottawa in 1955. That attitude of national disunity and misunderstanding on the part of some Canadians with regard to the others, may, in all fairness, scarcely be blamed on the C.C.F., which has never taken root in Quebec-unlike the Liberals who were maintained in power for 22 years thanks to that province.
I insist on the fact that our universities were and still are in need of money, and Quebec universities as much and maybe more than those of other provinces. However, the Liberals' method of offering that money as grants from Ottawa was definitely unacceptable to Quebec. Indeed, the procedure imposed, and not merely suggested, by the Liberal party, was both a mistake and a danger to national unity.
The fact that it seemed adequate in nine out of ten provinces did not make it more acceptable in the French province. That is why it was unanimously rejected by the government, the universities and the population of Quebec, while the taxpayers in that province were nevertheless compelled to pay taxes for the benefit of all Canadians but themselves, despite the well-established principle "no taxation without representation".
Under the present arrangement, we want all Canadians, whatever their racial origin or

their creed, to start off with equal opportunities. Our primary object is to offer all men and women in this country equal opportunity of winning university degrees enabling them to hold their own in the Canadian nation of tomorrow.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) was the first Canadian government leader to maintain that the French language and the culture that goes with it, are part of the basic liberties which are worth upholding, and this could never be accomplished so long as Quebec universities were compelled to exist under distressed abstention. That is why we have sought to develop a formula making for a fair treatment of both the taxpayers and the institutions of higher learning of Quebec. Consequently, this bill represents an arrangement based on the Canadian economic situation and the history background of the oldest Canadian province.
We realize that the population of the nine other provinces is satisfied with the system which has been in force up to now, but we offer an alternative, a realistic compromise allowing a province such as the province of Quebec, to grant to its university population the benefits which it was forced to refuse because of its scrupulous respect for the constitution and for autonomy.
An interesting feature of this alternative is that it is offered to any province which, of its own free will, wishes to avail itself of the new formula. Up to now, the province of Quebec has been the only one to do so, but any other Canadian province may act likewise if it sees some advantage in such a course of action.
Certainly, I do not suggest that the formula was easy to find or that we did not have many difficulties to overcome. But due to the good offices of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and to the good will of the Quebec premiers, we have succeeded.
At this point, I wish to pay a tribute to Messrs. Duplessis, Sauve and Barrette.
I know that during the debate on the resolution, the opposition spokesmen tried to suggest that one thing, and one thing only, barred the way to an earlier settlement: Mr. Duplessis' uncompromising attitude for all that concerned, directly or indirectly, the constitution of Canada.
Well, I remind the house with pleasure that the initial negotiations for the settlement of this question were entered into with

the hon. Mr. Duplessis. I do not want to lessen the extraordinary talent of Hon. Paul Sauve, whose very short term in office gave rise to so many hopes that are now becoming a reality. But I might say that Mr. Sauve, throughout his discussions with the federal government about the problem of aid to the universities of the province of Quebec, always stated that he was following in the steps of his predecessor whose thought he was only taking up again.
Last July, I personally had an opportunity to discuss with Premier Duplessis various propositions for the purpose of coming to an agreement.
A few days before his death, Mr. Duplessis stated that he would be in a position to submit, in October, a positive proposition to the ministers in Ottawa. It was the Hon. Paul Sauve who submitted that positive proposition. Federal ministers discussed it with Mr. Sauve and, at the time of his tragic death, only a few details remained to be worked out, which was done during a private interview between Mr. Antonio Barrette, Mr. Sauve's successor, and the Minister of Finance, sponsor of the bill which is now before us.
Therefore, we had claimed, under the Liberal administration, that it was possible to settle this problem in a constitutional way and to the satisfaction of the premiers of all the provinces. We have kept our word admirably, because Premier Barrette himself believes that this bill is consistent with the terms of Mr. Duplessis' proposal, which was submitted again by Mr. Sauve, and later by Mr. Barrette himself.
That solution was made possible through an increase in the provincial tax on corporations, deductible from the federal tax. Now the fact is that we were the promoters of the "deductibility" formula at the 1954 Conservative convention held in Ottawa. I remember defending the deductibility formula in the House of Commons, on April 26, 1954, when I replied to the arguments of the then minister of northern affairs and national resources, now leader of the Liberal opposition in Quebec, Mr. Jean Lesage.
The applause is rather muffled.
And those who would like to know exactly what was being claimed by the then Liberal minister, now disguised as a prophet of autonomy, and by the newborn infant of provincial autonomy, the hon. member for 79951-0-2084
Dominion-Provincial Relations Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), can read two enlightening articles by Mr. Clement Brown, in Le Devoir of Friday and Saturday last. Le Devoir's parliamentary correspondent reports fully, word for word, the very terms in which Mr. Lesage objected to the deductibility of provincial income tax from federal income tax.
1 am not afraid to say, as a federal minister, that this bill is the best possible way of solving the crisis for which the Liberals were responsible in the first instance. It is a formula which allows the province of Quebec to recover its place at the forefront of the provinces that form the confederation. It allows the universities of Quebec to develop and prosper like all institutions of higher learning in the other provinces of Canada.
If we now go back to twenty five years ago, we realize that, between 1936 and 1960, the old province of Quebec has developed more than it did between the time of the discovery of Canada and 1936. Thanks to Mr. Duplessis' energetic and bold policy, it has become a great provincial state and an industrial giant.
Messrs. Sauve and Barrette took over from their predecessor and, in less than a year, gave the province of Quebec a new trend, under the impetus of their personal leadership. That is why the provincial session which has just come to a close in Quebec city, will go down in history as the session of education.
The new leader of the Union Nationale has managed to come to an agreement with Ottawa and to obtain from our government the share which, by right, belonged to the universities of Quebec. The hon. Mr. Barrette introduced three bills in the Quebec legislature, one to recover the money accumulating in the coffers of the conference of universities, the second to increase provincial grants to Quebec universities, and the third to raise the income tax of business concerns to provide funds for education in Quebec.

Now, in this case, the money was here in Ottawa, and it was up to the Quebec government to take the lead and ask the Ottawa government to settle the problem. Finally, it was settled, but in a haphazard
26, 1960
Dominion-Provincial Relations way, as I will show in the course of my remarks. A settlement is proposed, but what type of settlement?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: That is under a Conservative government.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I would have liked the Solicitor General to say a word about the bill and to tell us what he thinks about it. The purpose of the bill submitted to us is twofold. First, we are asked to extend for two years the rental of the provincial share of income tax; then, the bill provides an arrangement between Canada and the provinces for the sharing of corporation income tax with regard to federal government grants to universities.
I want to deal with this latter proposal, Mr. Speaker, because this proposed amendment is something new in this bill. At the resolution stage of this bill, several members spoke feelingly of autonomy or rather told us that the field of education belongs to the provinces. We all know that, Mr. Speaker, and besides, it is guaranteed by the constitution.
Others told us with deep emotion about the furrow of education in Quebec that the late premier had ploughed, a furrow that had been dug by someone else.
I agree, Mr. Speaker, that this cannot be made a matter of sentiment. It is a problem of common concern to the federal government and to the provinces. We have to face it as a whole, and know what it is all about.
This bill offers the provinces to take 1 per cent on corporation taxes and to subsidize their universities at the rate of $1.50 per capita out of the tax proceeds. If, however, the amount thus collected at the rate of $1.50 per capita is in excess of that allowed and worked out by the federal government, the surplus collected by the province shall be deducted from equalization payments.
Where the amount collected by a province is less than $1.50 per capita, the federal government will make up the difference.
However, for this agreement to come into effect and to become law, it is necessary, as mentioned in section 9a, paragraph (b), subparagraph ii, of the act that,
satisfactory arrangements exist in the opinion of the minister for the payment by the province directly to institutions of higher learning in the province, of amounts by way of grants.
It is therefore essential, under that act, that money collected from corporations by

Dominion-Provincial Relations the province be affected to universities, and the federal government grants this permission on the understanding that this obligation will actually be fulfilled.
It follows, therefore, that if the minister is not satisfied with the use made of the moneys collected from corporations, he may withdraw the offer he makes under this act, and resume his taxation power over corporations.
In the final analysis, the federal government decides, when a provincial tax is decreed, what its rate will be, what provincial purpose it will serve and what it will yield to the provincial treasury.
Those conditions, Mr. Speaker, are onerous and are an encroachment on the autonomy of the provinces.
The formula we are being asked to approve is different from the old formula proposed by the government of Mr. St. Laurent and which was deemed unacceptable.
Under the previous formula, the universities were free to accept unconditionally the grants which were offered to them and to spend the money as they liked.
The formula of the St. Laurent government merely gave a definition of a university under the terms of the act, in order to limit the institutions which were to receive those grants. Indeed had the word "university" not been defined, some institutions or schools would have claimed their rights to those grants and we should have had confusion and imbroglios.
I want to rectify an article published in Le Devoir of April 9, 1960, under the signature of its correspondent, Mr. Brown, in which the latter stated that under the formula submitted by the St. Laurent government the minister of finance was "the ultimate judge with regard to grants, in that he was given the tremendous power of defining university education, universities, etc.," and there the author of the article stops, without going any further.
I have to tell that correspondent that his statement was false and inaccurate, because the formula submitted by the St. Laurent government did not at all define university education.
I have here before me the agreement concluded in 1957, between the then minister of finance (Mr. Harris) and the national conference of universities, and paragraph 8 gives a definition of the words "population", "province", "student", "university", "university de-

gree", "university level", but there is no definition whatsoever of the expression "university education".
Since that agreement was renewed in January 1960, between the present Minister of Finance and the Canadian universities foundation, the same definition of the words "population", "student", "university", "university degree", "university level", can be found under paragraph 13, but there is not a single word tending to define the expression "university education".
Some of the terms used in the 1957 convention have been renewed in the 1960 agreement, which was signed by the present Minister of Finance.
I wonder if the correspondent of Le Devoir wanted to mislead his readers or whether he thought they knew nothing about this, but I can tell him, without having reached the degree of intelligence and superiority which he assumes for himself, that we are able to read a text, that we know the definition of certain words, and that we can tell an insect from an animal.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I must say the present Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance have been logical; that they have never attacked the constitutionality of the law; that they never claimed that it encroached upon provincial laws.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) quoted the words spoken by the Minister of Finance in the house, in 1958, as reported in Hansard. I should like to repeat what the hon. member for Laurier said, but since the time at my disposal is limited, I will merely say that the hon. member for Laurier was repeating the very words spoken by the Minister of Finance, in 1958.
Here is what he actually said in 1960:
As long as this government directs the destinies of this country, it will never interfere in the field of education, which comes under provincial jurisdiction.
That has always been his position, frank and clear. We knew where we stood.
But, considering his attitude today, we can well wonder whether the Minister of Finance has not changed his mind. Does he not see in his bill some interference on the part of his government in the provincial field?
The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) has told us about the needs of universities-we

know all about those needs-and he has told us about the unacceptable formula submitted at the time of the Liberal regime, but to which, however, no counter proposal was ever made. He also referred to the crisis brought about by the Liberals. But I wonder whether it would not have been better for him to tell us about this bill and to tell us what he thinks about it. I also ask the other Quebec ministers, including the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) whom I see in his seat, and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) whether they consider that the St. Laurent formula worked against provincial autonomy? Is the present formula not more dangerous?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: That is an invitation.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The ministers do not speak with one voice.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The other point I wish to raise, and which I mentioned in fact at the outset of my remarks is that the excess amount collected by the province which chooses to exercise its option of collecting 1 per cent of the corporation tax will be deducted from the equalization payments to the province.
In other words, the province will become a tax collector for the federal government. The federal government says to the provinces: I authorize you to collect this tax, I order you to use it in such a way, and if you collect more than the amount agreed between us, you will return the balance to me in one form or another.
I would have liked the Solicitor General to discuss that aspect of the bill and tell us his views on the matter.
The hon. member for Laurier, a moment ago, quoted judgments from the supreme court of which I have a copy here. I shall refrain from going back over that, because I do not want to take up too much of the house's time. However, under the constitution, the provinces have the right to raise direct taxes for provincial purposes and to spend them as directed by the legislature. This also holds true for the federal government, which can raise any tax for its own purposes and spend the proceeds as directed by parliament.
That question has been settled by our courts and I shall not refer to it again.
The hon. member for Laurier quoted the judgment of Mr. Justice Estey-and Mr. Justice Taschereau and Mr. Justice Kerwin
Dominion-Provincial Relations share that opinion-to the effect that no province nor the federal government may become each other's collection agency.
On the basis of that judgment of the supreme court, if a province cannot transfer its powers of taxation to the central government, it follows by implication that it cannot take orders or enter into any agreement limiting its powers, because in so doing it is surrendering part of its prerogatives.
That would seem to us a breach of section 92 of the constitution which provides that the central government has no right to direct taxation money levied for provincial purposes.
In fact, such tax levied for provincial purposes belongs exclusively to the provinces.
It was said that this bill is an improvement on the old formula and is a step in the right direction; I do not agree. On the contrary, I suggest the bill is a flagrant interference by the federal government in provincial affairs and a step, not in the right direction, but a serious and dangerous step backwards.
The provincial government has no right to act as the agent of the federal government to collect a tax, and the latter has no right to limit the provincial government in its taxation powers.
We all know that universities need money and particularly those of Quebec who were starving and were longing for the money put aside for them by the conference of universities. They are glad today to recover what belongs to them, but if they are able to do so, it is because a wise and farsighted government, under the leadership of the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, had included a provision allowing those sums to be put aside so that our institutions could collect them when they decided to do so, and this, without any directions on the way to use them.
This bill includes formalities and obligations that I have already mentioned and which make it the worst encroachment on provincial autonomy. If this is the result of the word "autonomy" that we have heard during many years at every turn and in all occasions, that result is quite poor and small. I say that this bill is a bad bargain.
I would like to hear the other ministers from Quebec explain their stand on this matter, since the Solicitor General mentioned it a few moments ago.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how the Quebec ministers would be able to justify their stand

Dominion-Provincial Relations in the face of the thesis they defended? They may say that universities today have the money they wanted-and that is true-but I shall answer that they have it at a price they denounced as dangerous, as an infringement of autonomy, not to mention the fact that if they voted in favour of this bill, they will trample under foot all the principles they advocated. If the ministers from Quebec are trying to refloat the Union Nationale by means of that legislation, they have not much to offer to that party. The effect might not be as considerable, nor as efficient as they thought.

speechtext:
It often happens, Mr. Speaker, that the desired result is not achieved, they try by every means to make us forget the disastrous policy of the Quebec government, and that is why somebody well known and close to the Prime Minister organized the visit of the premier of Quebec to Toronto, to show the people of that city that the Union Nationale party is not as noxious as it has been said or described to be.
Mr. Speaker, I shall vote for the maintenance of the payment of 13 per cent of the income tax to the provinces; but, with regard to the option offered the provinces in respect of university grants, I cannot accept it in its present form, and it should be modified su as to safeguard provincial autonomy. Autonomy is a big word which has been preached and the meaning of which has been developed over the years. I cannot vote in favour of this bill, in its present form, because it is dangerous and far-reaching, and because it affects provincial autonomy in a most serious way.

speechtext:
One moment, please. You asked me a question and you would like

me to answer it. What does "totonomy" eat in winter? I have not the slightest idea what "totonomy" eats but I know that at this time and as a result of Union Nationale "totonomy" there are in Quebec some 200,000 unemployed, and in Montreal alone 80,000. If the province of Quebec had all the money owed to it by the federal government and that it did not receive because of that "totonomy", well, there would be less unemployment in Quebec.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this matter, several interesting speeches were delivered by talented speakers from both sides of the house. I must say, however, that interest does not necessarily mean truth. For many reasons, I should like today, on behalf of the electors of the constituency I represent, to express my views on this Bill C-56, concerning education.
One of those reasons, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that I represent a constituency where is located one of the finest institutions of higher learning in Canada, Laval University of Quebec city.
Mr. Speaker, do not fear that in saying this, I am having an embarrassing superiority complex, but be assured that I feel a deep and legitimate pride. Besides, I know that other fine universities exist in Canada, and to name but one, I will mention the University of British Columbia, which I visited about a fortnight ago with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor). All Canadians must also be proud of that university, especially western wanadians, because it is an institution dating from the second half of the nineteenth century and which has known, ever since, a continuous, glorious and successful development.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary to stress any further the idea that education is, beyond any doubt, a provincial responsibility. The present government, through the voice of several of its ministers, time and again has clearly expressed its opinion on the matter, and the provincial authorities, at least in principle, have given their agreement. There is no doubt also, in my humble opinion, that the fathers of confederation were thinking of the universities when they put education under provincial jurisdiction, since several subsidized universities already existed at that time.
Besides, the term "education", to use philosophical language has an intention that goes much beyond what we call instruction, and applies to the whole training process

leading to information and physical and moral formation of the individual. How then could we limit the term education when referring to university grants, and apply it only to primary and secondary schools?
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the term education, as it is used in the confederation act, applies, in my opinion, to university education, and the Liberal government should have taken that theory into account, when it set up the university grant system. Be that as it may, I will limit my remarks to the principle of the bill we are now considering.
Under this bill, the provinces would have an opportunity to pay the grants themselves by raising their own corporation tax. In my humble view, an important aspect of this legislation is the Conservative government's care to abide by the 1867 confederation pact by handing back to the provinces the possibility of raising the taxes required to meet the needs of universities through the deduction of a provincial tax from the federal tax.
Mr. Speaker, probably a number of Liberals will find weaknesses in this formula, but it is acceptable. Furthermore, it must be pointed out that we are repairing an old building which had been badly put together in the first place. The legislation is fantastic, to borrow an expression from the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), but it is legislation that it is long overdue.
In short, the true situation is not as described by the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Meunier) who said that the provincial government will be the agent of the federal government. After all, what has the provincial government done, or rather, what has the federal government said? It has said: I give you the right to raise taxes. What has happened in fact is that the government of the province of Quebec, at least, has raised a tax and, for the first time in 25 years, the federal government has withdrawn from that field of taxation so as to abide by the spirit of the Canadian constitution.
What is surprising in all the discussions about this matter is the obvious about-face of certain Liberal authorities. Just to prove it, I should like to recall certain statements made by Mr. Jean Lesage, which are quoted in part by Clement Brown in an article which appeared in Le Devoir for April 23, 1960. I quote:
In his speech of April 14, 1954, Mr. Jean Lesage described as consistent with the constitution "the distribution among the provinces of taxation revenues... by parliament". He quoted a few figures in support of his view.
However, Mr. Lesage added: "I think that nobody will deny that, in order to maintain our system of government, every level of government must have the financial resources it needs to fulfil Its constitutional obligations".
The Liberal leader then went on to say that in the absence of federal grants, certain have not
Private Bills-Divorce
provinces would not be able to meet their needs.
With regard to the tax legislation on personal incomes enacted by the Duplessis government, Mr. Lesage made the following distinction: (1) first, there is the tax legislation itself, and Quebec is entitled to enact it; (2) then there is the matter of the federal deduction of the new provincial tax, something to which Ottawa cannot agree.
Speaking to the Minister of Finance, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said, as reported at page 4726 of Hansard of September 6, 1958:
When he says they would welcome a formula which would make it possible for Quebec to accept this kind of assistance, I can assure him that when we were in office certainly we would have welcomed any formula which would have made that possible; indeed, we certainly sought such a formula.
May I add, Mr. Speaker, that I was surprised to hear another Liberal voice, that of the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) say the words we find at page 2816 of Hansard of April 1, 1960:
It is my understanding that only the tax collector is changed, and nothing else.
Would the hon. member deny or consider only very lightly the theory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who said "it does not make sense that a government should collect the revenues while another spends them".
Why, Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member not repeat also the theory of his former colleague, Mr. Lesage, that "to maintain our system of government, each level must have the financial resources it needs to fulfil its constitutional obligations?" I will repeat, Mr. Speaker, that in the principles and in practical application, the Conservative government has always been and is still the best safeguard of the rights of the provinces and may I add that this bill will benefit all the provinces which will want to take advantage of it.
I would not want to let this opportunity go by without, as a member from the province of Quebec, putting the record straight following the very unfair remarks made by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napier-ville (Mr. Dupuis) on April 1, 1960 and which we find at page 2831 of Hansard. I quote:
I cannot help remembering all the years we lost, when our young people might have enjoyed a university education which was refused them, under the pretext of protecting a sham autonomy.
Would this mean, Mr. Speaker, that for having refused the federal grants to universities, the provincial government failed to fulfill its obligations towards our universities? It is not quite the testimony of a former rector of Laval University, which I find in L'Evenement Journal, of Friday June 13, 1958. Here is what Msgr. Ferdinand Vandry, vice-rector of Laval University, said at that time:
"It is a mistake", said Msgr. Vandry, "for the press to make so much out of the federal government's

Private Bills
grants to Canadian universities, and a mistake to contend that we should accept those grants. Those grants amount to almost nothing compared to what we get from the provincial government, which, thanks to the broadmindedness and understanding of Mr. Duplessis, has made Laval what it is today."
And Msgr. Vandry goes on to say: "I have been the rector of this university for nine years, and I am now in a position to state that over a period of ten years the provincial government has given Laval University a total of $22,000,000. I think that those are things that should be said, because we must say them. The initiator of the 'Cite Uni-versitaire', Msgr. Vandry added, is actually and truly Mr. Duplessis himself."

Mr. Chairman, as I understand this bill, this company is almost identical in name with another insurance company called Canadian Reinsurance Company, the only difference being in the one case the word "Reassurance" is used and in the other "Reinsurance" is used. I think this is an objectionable practice and one that ought to be discontinued. I am aware that this is done with the full knowledge of the superintendent of insurance, and I am aware that the

owners of the companies are common owners. Since they are set up as separate corporate entities, however, they need not continue to have a common ownership. There is no obligation in that respect. This is a practice that I think is thoroughly bad and ought to be discouraged. There should be a distinctive name that is not confusing with other company names granted incorporation by this parliament.
There is one other practice that I find objectionable. It is no longer the practice in the incorporation of these companies to clear the names, to find out and report to parliament whether or not the name is objectionable from the point of view of similarity to other companies incorporated by letters patent. This practice was followed for a great number of years where incorporation took place by a special act. It was left, of course, to parliament or the appropriate committee of parliament to deal with it and decide whether or not a charter would be granted regardless of the similarity of names. This information was brought forward for the consideration of the committee concerned with the particular bill or for parliament itself. The discontinuance of that practice is something which, I think, should not be allowed to pass unnoticed.
I have no particular objection to this bill. I am merely seizing the opportunity of raising these two matters which I think are of importance.
