maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. S-20, respecting British Columbia Telephone Company-Mr. Jung-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Acquisition of shares.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY
speechtext:
This bill was debated at the second reading stage and a good deal of evidence was given concerning it when it was before the standing committee. I am concerned with only one very narrow point and it is this. I must say that the charter of the British Columbia Telephone Company is a somewhat confusing document to understand. I therefore put forward my views with some hesitation. I defy anyone to be very precise and clear in his opinion of the exact legal position of that company after reading the relevant legislation concerning it.
In any event, it has been stated in debate in all of the three places where this bill was discussed that its immediate purpose was to enable the British Columbia Telephone Company to acquire another company operating in British Columbia, namely Northwest Telephone Company. As far as I am concerned, I have no objection whatever to that procedure. There can be no objection, as I see it, to the purpose of this bill as stated.
The British Columbia Telephone Company charter, as I read it, limits the British Columbia Telephone Company to constructing and operating lines in British Columbia. Then
3296	HOUSE OF
Private Bills	^ <- T>
it has some incidental powers to acquire connecting lines going outside the province. But section 9 of the relevant legislation enables it to acquire shares in companies having similar objects. The bill now before us seeks to clarify that section 9 in order to make it clear-because it was not clear formerly- that section 9 enables it to acquire all the shares of any company or to acquire another company by purchase of its shares.
But the difficulty as I see it or the narrow point which concerns me is this. Both the British Columbia Telephone Company and indeed the company it seeks to acquire are largely United States owned corporations. I have no immediate objection to that fact. I recognize the need for foreign capital in this country as well as does anyone else. But by this amendment we are putting this British Columbia company in the position where it can go anywhere throughout the whole of Canada and acquire, through this amended bill, any other telephone companies in Canada.
There are many hundreds of telephone companies in all the other provinces of Canada except the three prairie provinces. It seems to me that a question of principle is involved as to whether or not-with the increased importance of telecommunications, with the developments of the last ten years and particularly their military significance-we are going to enable a foreign-owned and controlled company to acquire other companies and thus establish a network system across this country.
I think it is elementary to point out that our regulatory control of telephone companies-inasmuch as there is any control- is through the board of transport commissioners and the Railway Act. Indeed, the legislation refers to the Railway Act. I of course hold the view that with the changes that have come in this whole field in the postwar years, particularly in the last ten years, it is necessary to have that whole area reexamined or re-appraised and the appropriate changes made in the general legislation on this subject.
Certainly I would ask the government whether or not they have considered the question of principle raised by this amended bill. I should like to have their views. I have put my own views forward with some hesitation on the subject because, as a result of the old draftsmanship-perhaps I had better say that instead of "confusing"-of some of the clauses in the special act incorporating British Columbia Telephone Company there is a considerable degree of obscurity. If I am right in reading the amending bill now before us as enabling this company, which by its own charter is limited to British Columbia,

I think it is something that the government ought properly to look at. The government has an obligation to the House of Commons to give its views on this point before the bill passes. I have no objection to any other features in the bill; I have just that one narrow point which I think should be considered and dealt with.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have had the privilege of discussing this point with the hon. member for Ottawa West and I am grateful to him for having discussed this matter again before this committee. In view of what he has said about the complicated nature of the incorporating act, it would be almost an impertinence for a junior counsel like myself to dispute anything said by the hon. member who is a very eminent counsel. But because of the discussions that I have had with the hon. member for Ottawa West I took the opportunity of discussing this matter not only with the parliamentary agent of the company but also with the officials of the company itself.
I have been assured by the parliamentary agent that the question of the proposed expansion does not derogate in the slightest from the original principle of the incorporating act, and the original principle is not being altered by the bill. If it may satisfy the hon. member, I have a telegram which I received from the British Columbia Telephone Company which reads as follows:
Douglas Jung, M.P., Parliament Bldgs., Ottawa, Ont.
The company has no intention of enlarging its operations beyond the powers which it presently holds. It does however propose to extend northward into the Yukon to Alaska.
British Columbia Telephone Co.
I think there was no withholding of information. The company frankly and honestly answered all questions put to it in the standing committee. It noted that it wished to take over the operations of the Northwest Telephone Company, and I think it would be a physical impossibility at this time for the company to come east and take over any or all of the 4,500 other telephone companies now in operation in Canada. From my discussions with the hon. member for Ottawa West I think he is more concerned with the rapid changes in communication and the fact that our legislation has not kept pace with this aspect. I think the hon. member has taken this opportunity to put his views on the record and I agree with him. It may be that in time we may have to set up a different board of control to look into communications, but for the purposes of this bill

we must limit our discussion to the clause under discussion and I hope that what I have said this afternoon will satisfy the hon. member for Ottawa West.

I do not know whether the government has considered the point or not. I wish they would. (Translation):

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS-EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, towards the end of this afternoon's discussion on this bill, I had been quoting the testimony of a former rector of Laval University about the generous treatment received by Quebec universities during the period when the provincial government refused to accept federal grants.
To the figures I then mentioned I now wish to add that, since 1945, the Quebec government has paid to universities in my province the substantial amount of $112,036,297.38.
This continuing policy on the part of the government which was then headed by the hon. Mr. Duplessis, is, I feel, adequate proof of the consideration he gave to university education.
Before resuming my seat, I must express my regret with regard to some parts of the speech made in this house on April 1, 1960 by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). I am sorry that, because of a lack of information rather than ill intent, the hon. member, when dealing with Canadianism, should have spoken of the existence of a superiority complex in French Canada.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
As a matter of fact, I do not see that many provinces, besides Quebec, have shown greater broadmindedness and greater respect for minorities.
No one can fairly claim that French-speaking Canadians have at any time tried to impose their language or their religion on the minorities which have chosen to live in Quebec.
I should like to quote here a page from a speech delivered by the Rev. Father Georges Desjardins, a Jesuit, on the treatments of minorities. Here is what he said in his book entitled: Quebec Schools
Other racial groups, upon settling in Canada, have had to accept the existing legislation. When they arrive in Quebec, immigrants find a confessional and Christian school system, either Catholic or Protestant, which has been officially recognized as such since 1846, but which in fact existed long before that date. They must therefore choose between Catholic or Protestant schools. The Jews have chosen Protestant schools. They are therefore regarded as Protestants for the purposes of distribution, as between Catholic and Protestant school boards, of provincial and municipal grants, and also of the undenominational tax (corporation tax).
The Quebec government has been so generous in the sharing of such grants and taxes that Protestant boards have, from time to time, been favoured to the detriment of Catholic boards which every year lose considerable revenues to which they are entitled. In any event, Jews have received from Catholic Quebec the maximum positive rights they could be granted. Under the tradition of the province, they can also require the authorities of Protestant schools attended by their children to arrange for the latter to receive the religious education to which they are entitled under natural law.
As regards Catholic minorities-Irish, English, Scottish, Italian, Hungarian, Syrian and others- they have always received a very liberal treatment from the Catholic committee on education and from Catholic school boards. None of those minorities pay double tax. All their children are educated at the expense of the Catholic taxpayers, without any racial discrimination.
In support of this, I might quote the words of an English-speaking Protestant, Mr. James Patton, secretary of the Quebec Protestant teachers' association. Here is what he said:
(Text):
We are well treated here. We get our full share of tax money. The Catholics go out of their way to be fair and even generous to us. We are only embarrassed because the Roman Catholic schools in other provinces do not get the same break-*
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I believe those things should be mentioned in this house so that the province of Quebec may be considered as it should be, that is to say as an asset within the Canadian confederation.
As regards the bill we have been discussing since the beginning of this sitting, I shall merely sum up my views in saying that the present government has agreed to withdraw from a taxation field in which the provincial

government can itself levy income which will have to be granted to universities.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that giving the provinces the taxation rights they need to fulfil their purposes is indeed the best way to respect the confederation pact.
May I say, in conclusion that the universities are, so to speak, the cultural yardstick of a people and that both the federal and provincial governments must protect their interests.
However, Mr. Speaker, it is also necessary that our people continue to live in an atmosphere of good understanding and harmony, for the safeguard of the Canadian confederation. The action taken by the present Conservative government is such as to achieve that purpose, and we commend the government for having done so.

The grant at that time amounted to 50 cents per capita and, in 1951-52, all the universities and every province in Canada accepted those grants.

In 1956, however, when the Liberal government, headed by the Right Hon. The Supreme Court of Canada has rendered a decision providing that when a province levies a direct tax for provincial purposes, the federal government has no right to claim any share of the moneys collected by the province. According to me, this bill is unconstitutional and unless the government gives an explanation to my satisfaction, I shall withhold my decision on this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions, since I have had the honour of being elected to this house, and particularly in the debate on the resolution which preceded this piece of legislation, I expressed my views as clearly as possible


on the precedent which was created in 1951 by the federal government of the time.
I tried to show, both by historical facts and by references to the constitution, that the principle then established represented a serious mistake, and that only the provinces had rights and obligations in educational matters, at every level of the educational system.
I also emphasized the serious danger that Quebec was likely to run into had it yielded on that point.
In order to avoid repetition, I shall therefore try today not to deal again with those angles of the problem, though they may be of capital importance in the establishment of a national unity consistent with the constitution.
Since then, I heard various views on the subject and in spite of my sincere and loyal efforts, I found nothing in them which might shake my position or any of the arguments I used in support of my position.
In consequence-though it may displease those who do not share my opinion, and with all due respect for the views of others-I want to confirm once more, at the very beginning of my remarks, that federal grants to our institutions of higher learning in this country are obviously inconsistent with the imperative principles of our constitution and contrary to the rights, powers and obligations which are an exclusively provincial field.
It is with this reservation that I wish to deal with the legislation now before us, which tends to lessen the singularly serious effects of the 1951 precedent with regard to the only province which, in this matter, offered a resistance that was all the more vigorous and consistent for its being based on history, on the constitution, and on the firm will to preserve full and complete freedom of action.
Everybody is familar with the background of that legislation. Since 1951, the federal parliament has been called upon to vote annual grants to our universities, and thus to by-pass the provincial governments which are exclusively responsible in the educational field.
That precedent, which has recurred each year ever since, has become a kind of institution, so much more difficult to uproot that nine provinces out of ten have accepted it without the least objection; in fact they even declared themselves favourable to it. Only Quebec has consistently rejected it. It so

happened, at a given moment, that the Quebec attitude did not please the authorities in Ottawa. By what means could its resistance be shaken?
So, in 1954, a method was resorted to which, it was hoped, would prove workable. It was stated that in so far as Quebec grants were concerned, they would accumulate in the treasury of the national conference of Canadian universities, in the obvious hope that such a Tantalus torment would give our institutions of higher learning such an appetite, would develop such an amount of gastric juice that in the end they would give in.
Fortunately, the nature and strength of the motives which had inspired Quebec were grossly misconstrued.
Beyond the purely material and financial point of view, there was a principle at stake, the principle of fiscal and constitutional liberties, a principle which, to a large extent, inspired the federative pact of 1867, and the ignoring of which would surely have brought about the abortion of the Charlottetown, Quebec and London conferences.
The accomplished fact brought about by that precedent of 1951 had none the less become a source of serious injustice towards the citizens of Quebec. Were they not contributing a large share of the taxes which were distributed in the other provinces by way of university grants?
Was there no possibility of a compromise that would take into account both the desires of the other provinces and the position so steadfastly held by the province of Quebec? Both the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the Quebec provincial authorities- who were also anxious to recover the share of taxes raised for provincial purposes, and to which in all fairness the province was entitled-devoted themselves to finding a compromise solution.
The legislation now before us is the outcome of those co-operative efforts. What does it amount to?
The best way to answer that question is to borrow the words of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), in the speech he delivered on March 18 last, as recorded on page 2229 of Hansard. Here is what he said:
In conclusion may I endeavour to summarize the effect of the legislation now proposed. In addition to assuring to the provinces till March 31, 1962 the benefit of the increase from 10 to 13 per cent in their share of the yield from the personal income tax, this measure will
26, 1960
Dominion-Provincial Relations
(a)	offer all provinces equally an alternative to the present system of federal assistance to universities in the knowledge that none of them will suffer any diminution in consequence of the adoption by its province of the alternative plan;
(b)	place both the present system and the new alternative system on a firm statutory basis for the next two years conterminous with the period of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act.
What is the nature of this alternative system referred to by the minister? It simply allows provinces which have made no arrangements with the federal government to rent their power to levy taxes on corporations or provinces which, though having entered into such an arrangement, now wish to terminate it with the federal government's concurrence, to receive an additional 1 per cent tax on corporations, a tax which can be deducted from the federal tax.
It may happen however, that the amounts recovered in this way by the provinces will either be greater than the amount that would have been paid to their universities by the federal government, or it may be less. In either case, there will be an annual adjustment, with the federal government either retaining the balance on equalization payments or adding to such payments to make up the amount. In that way, the provinces will receive equal treatment, without discrimination, whatever system they choose.
The essential requirement for any province to take advantage of this new system is that the province make satisfactory arrangements, in the minister's judgment, to pay its institutions of higher learning at least the equivalent of the sums they would have received if they had taken advantage of the method now in force. In other words, the province must actually discharge its obligations toward our universities.
Of course, this act is not perfect. It shows the effect of the factual conditions that brought it about. It stems from a precedent inherited by this government and for which the government must now make allowance, mainly in view of the attitude of nine of the ten provinces of the country.
Last year I pointed out those difficulties and I drew the fire of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), a delayed fire since it came several months after the remarks I had made on this matter. He had then described as illogical and irrational the remarks I had made to this effect. Today, he wanted to act as our mentor and dictate the course we should follow. I admit that I am not at all inclined to accept his counsel, particularly

Dominion-Provincial Relations
after the constitutional heresies that crammed the speech he made this afternoon. I will truly feel in better company if I follow the counsel given on July 21 last by the editor of Le Devoir, a paper which surely cannot be suspected of centralizing tendencies. Here are Mr. Gerard Filion's views on this matter:
The strongest argument is the will of the other provinces. Nine provinces want federal grants, as they want health insurance, as they want family allowances, as they want this and that. Therefore, no Quebec veto can impede progress.
Important remarks could be made in that respect and restrictions indicated as well. However, taking it for granted that the will of nine provinces must finally win over the veto of one, there is but one solution left-setting up a special system for that province. For there is nothing in the constitution to compel Canadian provinces to accept a single procedure every time a step forward is to be taken. Diversity has no built-in evil and it may even become an asset.
That brings back to me the time of the union. While that constitution had been evolved in order to unite the two Canadas on a legislative and an administrative basis, what happened instead was that, throughout the existence of that system, there were three groups of legislation: one for Lower Canada, one for Upper Canada and a third one for the Union, it being utterly impossible and unnatural to amalgamate our two ethnic groups.
May I add that contrary to the hon. member for Laurier, Mr. Filion has the advantage of not being a mere layman in the matter of provincial autonomy.
This text from Le Devoir also provides an opportunity to point out to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) how far we are from wanting to veto the stand taken by the other provinces. We readily understand that their interests are divergent and that they are entitled to hold views different from ours. It is ridiculous to imagine for a moment that we are attempting to impose on them a sort of one-way Canadianism steeped exclusively in our traditions, our customs and our aspirations.
But neither do we want reduced to a minimum the constitutional rights and freedoms which were granted to us by the act of 1867 and have enabled the province of Quebec to play its part as the centre of French culture in our country, a culture that is and will remain one of the elements absolutely essential to the existence and development of the Canadian people. And because the bill before us is along that line of thought, because it will enable the provinces which so desire to recover their power


of taxation for educational purposes, I do not hesitate at all to support it as an improvement which the province of Quebec may rightfully welcome.
Some people-and it was their privilege to do so-paid particular attention to certain details of this bill and saw in them serious encroachments upon provincial autonomy. For example they took exception to it because it leaves it to the minister to ascertain that the agreements reached by the universities and the provinces wishing to take advantage of this bill are really consistent with its provisions.
I admit that, at first, that requirement disturbed me and that I would have liked a better formula. But on that objection, which I discussed with some of my colleagues, I was told: Is it not up to the minister responsible for the administration of the act to find out whether or not facts are consistent with the provisions of that legislation and if the latter can therefore be put into effect? Otherwise, who would be responsible for it? Mr. Jean Lesage, who has suddenly become the fiercest autonomist, suggested that the Canadian universities foundation could act as an umpire. Mr. Lesage, who is burning today what he worshipped yesterday, and who actively took part in establishing the precedent which is at the very root of the difficulties we are now trying to solve, has, as I say, the ardent enthusiasm as well as the deficiencies of a neophyte. Is he not aware that there is such a thing as ministerial responsibility and that the only three instruments of the state are the legislative, the executive and the judiciary? What principle would allow us to ignore one of those three when there is a question of arbitrating a possible conflict between two opposed jurisdictions?
Mr. Lesage seems to have a rather failing memory. He was there, as a member of the cabinet when chapter 29, Statutes of Canada 4-5 Elizabeth II, to which this bill is related was passed in 1956. Let him read over closely each provision of that text and he will see the extent of the powers specifically given to the minister of finance, whether for the purpose of setting up equalization payments, or stabilization payments or of making any necessary adjustments.
What strikes me especially in this bill is the fact that from now on, the minister will have no control over the structure of our institutions of higher learning and over the required conditions to be eligible for grants. It will not be up to him anymore, as had been decided in 1952 by Mr. Lesage and his friends, to define the terms "university",

"student", "university degree", "university level". That problem will, from now on, be the responsibility of both the provinces and the educational institutions themselves.
This bill will therefore end such intrusions. While the Minister of Finance has the right to satisfy himself that the arrangements reached between the provinces and their universities are truly consistent with the requirements of the act-and it must be pointed out here that the term "arrangements" does not refer only to legislation, but has a much broader meaning-he will no longer, as in the past, be in a position to simply ignore the provinces, and to dictate directly to the universities the terms under which they may receive grants.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, that is a substantial and a very welcome gain. The Hon. Paul Sauve, whose political sense was justly commended by all, was the first to recognize this fact when, in his letter of December 14, 1959 to the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada, he wrote:
My colleagues and I are pleased with your decision to offer an alternative to the present system of federal grants to Canadian universities, to take better account of the letter of the British North America Act.
Another aspect of this measure is that it represents a temporary compromise. On that point also, Mr. Sauve expressed satisfaction in the following terms:
We are very happy that your letter indicates your intention to review the federal government policy in this matter, in the light of future discussions on the extent and nature of fiscal relations between the federal government and the provinces after March 31, 1962. It is therefore only a matter of considering a temporary modus vivendi which would obtain for the next two fiscal years only, that is until we take the decisions we shall be called upon to take and which will apply as of March 31, 1962.
The attitude of the late premier of the province of Quebec was, in this case, in keeping with the opinion of Rev. Father Ares, a prominent sociologist, whose authority in such matters could certainly not be questioned, and who, in January 1960, stated the following:
This is a solution which, in spite of its basic defect, deserves consideration on at least four counts: (1) it is probably, in the circumstances, the only possible solution, in view of the attitude of the other provinces, which insist on getting federal help: (2) it is essentially provisional, since its duration is fixed at two years, and that in 1962 everything must be reconsidered: (3) it is in line with autonomists' claims, since it recognizes -under certain conditions, of course-the rights of provincial governments to levy a special tax, deductible from federal tax, and to earmark such a tax for the financial upkeep of universities; (4) it paves the way to the settlement of an extremely
79951-0-209
Dominion-Provincial Relations
complex and delicate matter: that of the disposal of the sums which have been accumulating in Ottawa since 1952, in favour of Quebec universities.
At the purely practical level, that settlement affords Quebec invaluable advantages, and to convince oneself, one has only to consider provincial legislation passed during the last session, in anticipation of the provisional settlement assured by this measure. An educational fund had been set up in 1946, which was financed by miscellaneous sources. From now on, that fund will be increased by a tenth of the corporation tax, that is, for this fiscal year, by an approximate sum of $9,850,000. Out of that fund, in addition to the sums paid to school boards, as well as the basic grants which the universities and classical colleges are already getting, a payment of a sum equivalent to $1.75 per capita or 25 cents more than the proportion determined by the federal government will be provided for which will give a total amount of about $8,750,000.
At this point, a comment is in order, Mr. Speaker. In a conference he delivered recently before the students of Sir George Williams College, Mr. Lesage had in that respect the following remark to make:
What a glaring breach of Quebec autonomy it is to let Ottawa itself set the amount of provincial taxes to be collected for provincial purposes.
I should like to know on what basis Mr. Lesage can possibly make such a statement. Where, when and how did the federal government ever set the amount of taxes that Quebec is entitled to collect to meet its provincial obligations and deal with matters of its own jurisdiction? The fact that during its last session Quebec chose to set the amount to be levied for the universities at $1.75 instead of $1.50 per capita is the best possible denial of such a contention. Where Ottawa has actually placed a limit in its legislation is in the maximum deduction on its corporation taxes, just as the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent had done in 1956 by recognizing the principle involved, the very principle that had been so violently rejected two years before by Mr. Lesage himself.
Finally, to come back to the legislation recently voted in Quebec, I shall recall that a sinking fund was created to assist universities and affiliated colleges which wanted to proceed with expansion and development projects. These capital costs will be financed by income tax revenue, as well as by the $25 million accrued at the Canadian universities foundation and paid out to Quebec universities for retransmission to the

Dominion-Provincial Relations Quebec government, which is to use the money to this effect.
In other words, not only has Quebec rid its institutions of higher learning of a sword of Damocles hanging over their heads, but it made sure that henceforth there would be no more attempt on the part of the federal government to encroach upon the exercise of its rights, powers and obligations in respect of our educational establishments. From now on, it will carry out exclusively on its own the task deferred upon it, which consists in favoring the expansion of education and culture among the people for which it is responsible.
Mr. Speaker, those are the happy results of the compromise upon which rests the legislation now before us. That compromise has the advantage of deferring upon any province who would wish to do so, the responsibility of collecting on its own taxes for the financing of education without in the least hurting the financial and material interests of the other provinces. That seems to me a step in the right direction, a step towards the liberation from that kind of feudal system in which Ottawa has tried to keep the provinces of our dominion for the past 20 years.
Those considerations remind me of some statements made on December 17, 1940 to the Halifax Herald by one of the greatest statesmen of his time, the day after the publication of the Rowell-Sirois report, which is, to a considerable extent, the basis of the important change in the course of Canadian policy which took place at that. time. These are the terms and conditions under which the Hon. Mr. Cahan, former member of the Nova Scotia legislature, secretary of state in the Bennett government, and one of the highest legal authorities of his time, thought it possible to maintain responsible government in each one of this country's legislatures. I quote:
(Text):
I have always believed that dominion-provincial relations will only be placed on a stable basis when the provincial government is made responsible for raising the revenues which it annually expends. That should be the ideal basis of responsible selfgovernment. But this Sirois scheme makes the provinces more dependent upon grants and donations from the federal treasury, for the maintenance of provincial services.
The provincial legislature will come to exercise, year by year, the functions of a municipal council which is dependent, in matters of finance, upon the benefactions which it receives from the federal treasury. The dominion government will hold the purse, and financial control will gradually extend to the exercise of legislative and administrative control.
Many people would doubtless welcome that change, but the people of each province must decide for themselves whether the province shall become wholly dependent upon the dominion government,

or whether, in the administration of provincial affairs, the provincial government shall continue to maintain a considerable measure of independence, which is usually described as provincial autonomy. That raises an issue which the electors of each province must decide for themselves.
(Translation):
Those, Mr. Speaker, were the words of one of the most brilliant statesmen of his generation. Such words were the result of a fruitful experience in public affairs, extensive knowledge of Canada's history and constitutional law, and a sharp sense of reality.
Though they were spoken nearly 20 years ago, those words are still surprisingly up to date. In my view, they contain the doctrine that should inspire all our leaders, whatever their party and whatever the sphere of influence in which they are called upon to exercise their activity. In returning to the spirit and letter of the 1867 act, we shall be working to insure harmony and peace among the various groups that have to live side by side in this country.
It cannot be overemphasized that the 1867 constitution which, before being a piece of legislation enacted by the imperial parliament, was first an agreement reached between the four pioneer provinces of our Canadian homeland, had been carefully drafted by wise and enlightened statesmen endowed with remarkably sharp foresight. While very different in background, religious beliefs and political views, they united their efforts and goodwill in an attempt to put an end to the fratricidal struggles which, for so long, had pitted our forefathers against one another, and to secure for our two ethnic groups the rights and freedoms which would enable them to live together in harmony and to develop each according to its own traditions, culture and personality.
In so far as we remained faithful to the creative spirit of those great ancestors, we had every reason to be satisfied with the relations between the provinces and the central government, and with those between Canadians of Anglo-Saxon origin and Canadians of French origin. God grant that this teaching of history will not cease to guide us and to inspire us in the settlement of conflicts such as the one which the legislation before us today aims to bring to an end, as well as in the general administration of the public affairs of the country.
In this way, we shall be for the whole world an example of a great country where segregation, even in its most insidious form, has no hold on us, of a country different from all the others because of its particular

features, of a country that has remained faithful, both in spirit and in heart, to the two great civilizations from which it has risen and inherited such great and noble traditions.

Mr. Speaker, in recent years, I had become used, generally, to speak before the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion). Due to the tradition of alternation, it so happens to-night that I have to speak after him. I must tell you that this makes me very happy since I will have the opportunity to take up certain assertions he made about statements of mine in the past.
Until this afternoon, we believed on this side of the house that there were only two protectors of the constitution on the side of the Conservative members from Quebec. I refer to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) and the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion), who spoke just before me. But we realized this afternoon that we had a new protector of the Canadian constitution in my hon. friend and university classmate, the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer). I will come back a little later during my remarks to the statement my friend the Solicitor General made this afternoon about the constitution.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take up certain assertions, and to make the record straight about what I said previously in this house on the subject of university 79951-0-209'
Dominion-Provincial Relations grants. According to page 2648 of Hansard of April 13, 1959, unrevised English version, the hon. member for Sherbrooke referred to what I had previously said. He was then taking part in the debate on the budget and I had made a speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Well, on that occasion, in January 1959, I had given my views to the house on this matter of university grants. After having tried, in my humble way, to expound the Canadian constitution, I said the following that I quote from the speech of the hon. member for Sherbrooke:
Therefore, I repeat that in my opinion the fathers of confederation, in good faith, did not think in terms of universities when section 93 was enacted.
And according to what he said-I hope he did not have a text-the hon. member for Sherbrooke added:
Mr. Speaker, I must reply to that statement made by the member for Megantic that I have never heard such superficial and inadequate interpretation of the Canadian constitution.
And he went on ...
In 1867 in addition to Laval University_
I must say that, through the reference to that quotation which at that time seemed to be the very words of the hon. member for Sherbrooke, I realized when he spoke that I had read that somewhere. But the hon. member for Sherbrooke corrected himself a few days later and indicated that the text he mentioned referred to an article published in Le Devoir of March 14, 1959, over the signature of Mr. J. Rodolphe Thibodeau, under the heading: "The reader's views."
Both statements are absolutely identical. 1 do not want to insinuate, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Sherbrooke arrogated somebody else's writings to himself. I only want to point out that at that time he did not indicate that somebody else had written that in a newspaper.
I wish to refer to his statement that my interpretation was superficial and inadequate.
Since then, I have found that I am not the only one to have expressed that opinion and I have here the brief submitted by McGill University, in Montreal, to the royal commission on constitutional problems which, if I am not mistaken, was known as the Tremblay commission.
That brief does not carry any signature nor any indication of the author's name, but I have every reason to believe that it was drafted by somebody who is considered as an expert in constitutional law and who is precisely a professor in constitutional law at McGill University.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
As can be seen on pages 14 and 15 of the brief:
(Text):
Section 93 of the British North America Act makes no specific mention of universities nor does it touch upon the problem of financing their development. So far as we know, the subject of universities was not once discussed at any of the meetings of the fathers of confederation, and if we think of the situation that existed in Canada in 1867 we need not be surprised that the universities received so little consideration.
(Translation):
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, I was not the only one in 1959 to think that the fathers of confederation never had universities in mind when drafting the Quebec resolutions and later on the London resolutions which are the basis of the British North America Act.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I said in the beginning, I am privileged and sorry to see that the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) is not in his seat as I want to refer to what he said the first of April 1960 concerning the resolution when he referred to certain things I had said in January 1959.
I am now quoting the very words uttered on the first of April by the member for Bellechasse and which can be found in the French Hansard, page 2940:
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, contrary to what the hon. member for Megantic seems to think, Laval was not the only Quebec university in 1867.
And he then refers to what I had said in January 1959.
And Mr. Speaker, here is what I did say in January 1959. I quote from the English Hansard of January 20, 1959, page 133.
I had just expressed my humble opinion that the fathers of confederation had not foreseen in 1867 what could happen in 1950 or 1960 and I said:
Besides, if I am not mistaken, universities...
Universities, note the plural.
-at the time were private institutions. At least, it is a well known fact, in so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, where, for instance, Laval University has been established in 1852 by the Quebec seminary.
I did not refer then to the other universities which might have been established in the province of Quebec, namely McGill and Bishop's Universities, because I only mentioned Laval University as being a private institution.
An attempt was made, unwittingly I am sure, to restrict the import of the statement I made at that time.
Mr. Speaker, coming back to the topic which the hon. member for Bellechasse dealt with on April 1, 1960, in an effort to show that

Dominion-Provincial Relations Hon. James McGill, designed to establish in Montreal a high school which later became McGill University.
As regards the royal institution, the hon. member for Bellechasse quoted chapter 18 of the 1854 act. You will allow me, Mr. Speaker, to quote an act adopted in 1863, which is Act 26 Victoria, chapter 6, page 3 of the preface of the brief submitted by McGill University to the commission of inquiry on constitutional problems. I read the following:
(Text):
Under various acts of the legislature of the province of Quebec culminating in the act of 1863 (26 Viet. c. 26)-

Mr. Speaker, I see there is a mistake; it is not chapter 26, but chapter 6.
(Text):
-the board of governors of McGill University was also invested with the title and powers of the Royal Institution for the Advancement of Learning, which had been created by act of the legislature in 1801.
(Translation):
That means that as early as 1863 there no longer existed any royal institution, and the acts and authority of that institution had been handed over to McGill University. In 1867, when the British North America Act was drafted and agreed to in London, it was only fair that any money or property left by the royal institution, or if McGill University should later on become dependent on that foundation due to that act of the union, it should be returned to the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec.
However, there is more to it than that, Mr. Speaker. I have learned during my short experience that you must refer not only to legal documents but to their sources. Furthermore, in order to find out what certain legislators meant and, to a certain extent, to understand the Canadian constitution, the hon. member for Bellechasse could read the speeches made by the authors of that legislation, or any other. I find in a publication of the Public Archives of Canada, entitled Index to the Debates on Confederation, 1865, a foreword or introduction, written by professor Frank Scott to whom I referred a moment ago; but, this time, it is actually professor Scott who wrote this introduction, which I should like to paraphrase.
Professor Scott deplores the fact that there was no substantial report made of the Charlottetown conference, nor of the Quebec conference, nor of the speeches which were delivered there, except perhaps that which is reported in Confederation Documents, of 1895, which I quoted a moment ago.

After having deplored that, professor Scott adds, as recorded on page 7:
However, the general principles of federal union were hotly discussed on many occasions, both in parliament and on the hustings.
Then we read a sentence which is of no importance for the sake of my own argument. And professor Scott goes on to say:
However the researcher must consult the various parliamentary journals and the official reports if he wants to read up on the subject. After all, the parliamentary debates of Canada on confederation are the only copy and the only substantial and serious analysis of the project of a union and of the developments of that project until the end of the Quebec conference.
At page 9, the author goes on to say this:
We shall not reach unanimity on the value and the purport of those debates. The evidence, like any evidence of the kind, must be studied with care and used cautiously.
Farther down, the author says:
It is none the less very important evidence which acquaints with the thoughts, hopes and fears of the leaders of the time on confederation.
Mr. Speaker, I shall spare you some other representations that I might make because time is getting on.
With the help of this index which is very well made, I read in the report of the debates that took place in 1865 the speeches of those who attended the conferences of Charlottetown and Quebec.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I shall not quote everything I read because I ran through all the parts where mention was made of education and schools, and nowhere did I find any reference to universities and institutions of higher learning. However, mention was made of Catholic confessional schools, of dissident schools, of public schools and of separate schools, and it is the only reason, in my opinion, why paragraph 6 of the forty third resolution was enacted. It reads as follows:
(Text):
Education, saving the rights and privileges that the Protestant and Catholic minorities in both Canadas may possess as to their denominational schools at the time that the union comes into operation.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, in the light of paragraph 6 of resolution 43 which later became section 93 of the British North America Act, we see that the only concern of the fathers of confederation, and of all those who studied the 72 resolutions was the safeguard of the minority in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, in order to allow them to keep the school system that had been instituted in each of these provinces.
Mr. Speaker, having quoted those facts, I believe that if the hon. member for Bellechasse had a right to conclude that the fathers

of confederation had necessarily thought of universities in drafting those texts, I have a right also to come to the conclusion I drew last year. Besides, I am not the only one to come to this conclusion. May I remind you, however, of the words quoted at the beginning of my remarks.
But there is more. As I said before, I am not the only one to think so, and I would quote in this respect what Rev. Father Egide-M. Roy, of the minor brothers, said in 1924, in his book entitled "The development of the French-Canadian school system". I read it after I had expressed my views on the matter last year, Mr. Speaker. This is what Rev. Father Roy has to say on page 231:
In order to give some idea of education in the province of Quebec, we must first put aside secondary and higher education, i.e. classical colleges and universities. These institutions have been developed under the sole leadership of the clergy and they remained outside all governmental action or influence. They are private corporations, with their own identity. If for the past few years, they have been receiving grants-which are anyhow rather meagre-they nevertheless keep their complete independence.
That was what Rev. Father Roy said in 1924, Mr. Speaker, and I believe that conditions have not changed, either in 1951 nor in 1957 nor in 1960.
I therefore think, Mr. Speaker, that I am entitled to express my humble opinion and to conclude that the central government, or rather the central parliament, has a perfect right to vote grants to the universities without encroaching on provincial autonomy in the educational field.
There is an important distinction to be made between the power to grant subsidies -or make gifts-and the authority to legislate in educational matters.
And this is what I find on page 17 of the brief submitted by McGill University:
(Text):
Much confusion, has arisen in discussion of this subject through a failure to distinguish between

the power to spend crown moneys on behalf of education and the power to make laws in relation to education.
(Translation):
There is a basic difference between distributing sums of money collected by way of direct taxation in the federal field, and the power to legislate in the field of education.
Under the Liberal formula, the government of the time placed no condition on the use to be made of the funds distributed, it had no controlling authority over the administration of universities; it exercised no influence in the drafting of curricula or in the choice of teachers. In fact, all that was done at the time, that is in 1951, and since, was to determine the amount of money to be given by the federal government to institutions of higher learning, both in the province of Quebec and in the other Canadian provinces.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of my remarks, I think we have reached an appropriate time to ask you to call it ten o'clock.
